items.title: EU Emission Trading System applying to offshore vessels from 1 January 2027
items.original_title: EU Emission Trading System applying to offshore vessels from 1 January 2027
items.summary: Introduction From 1 January 2027, the application of the EU ETS Directive (EU ETS)[2] will extend to include offshore vessels of 5,000 GT or above. Already, since 1 January 2026, the maritime scope of EU ETS has not only included CO₂ emissions alone, but also methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O) emission. So, from 2027 onwards offshore shipping companies will have to surrender EU Allowances (EUAs) in respect of CO₂, methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions for all their ships that call at a port within the EEA commercially. If an offshore vessel calls at an EEA port for non-commercial reasons, e.g., obtaining supplies, a ship being in need of assistance or in distress, taking shelter from adverse weather, or it being rendered necessary by search and rescue activities, etc., then such port call is not deemed to be a ‘port of call’ for the purposes of the EU ETS, provided that no commercial operation takes place during that same call.

items.summary: French shipping giant CMA CGM more than tripled its third-quarter net profit as higher container freight rates and strong cargo volumes boosted earnings amid ongoing disruptions to global shipping routes in the Middle East. The Marseille-based group reported Friday that net income attributable to the group climbed to $2.32 billion in the third quarter of 2026, up from $760 million a year earlier, an increase of approximately 205%. Revenue rose 31.1% to $18.4 billion, while earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) jumped 61.6% to $4.78 billion. The strong results were driven primarily by CMA CGM’s container shipping business, which benefited from sustained demand and elevated freight rates as Middle East tensions continued to disrupt maritime trade routes and global supply chains. The figures underscore how ongoing disruptions in the Middle East are reshaping the container shipping market, supporting freight rates even as carriers face longer voyages, higher operating costs and changes to established trade routes. CMA CGM also expanded its terminal network through a partnership involving Terminal 4 at Saudi Arabia’s Port of Jeddah and the acquisition of a 49% stake in Morocco’s Nador Container Terminal. Looking ahead, CMA CGM expects strong container shipping demand to continue over the coming months , with freight rates that have been rising since the second quarter supporting the business.

items.summary: Germany’s 2027 budget passed its final committee stage overnight, leaving most of the cuts to rail freight support untouched. Terminal funding escaped, but track access subsidies did not, with operators stating they are ‘utterly baffled’ by why, after fierce campaigning, they still face a claimed 75% jump in network costs from next month. The Bundestag’s budget committee approved the 2027 federal budget in the early hours of Friday 13 November, after a session that ran until 5:55am, ahead of a final vote by the full parliament later this month. The cuts were first unveiled in the federal government’s summer draft budget in July, triggering four months of intense lobbying by rail freight groups to overturn them in parliament. “Knowingly burdening users in industry and trade and encouraging the shift to road is short-sighted and an affront to businesses and people alike.” The broader €25.35 billion transport budget saw steep cuts elsewhere, however, with 2027 investments for federal highway operator Autobahn GmbH slashed by €1.98 billion to €2.38 billion, alongside a €5.5 billion reduction in future commitment authorisations. Prior to the vote, terminal operator Contargo , together with members of combined transport research body SGKV, had called for at least €120 million in 2027 and €150 million in 2028, plus significantly higher commitments for 2028 to 2030.

items.title: From ocean liner to artificial reef: A warning for container shipping
items.original_title: From ocean liner to artificial reef: A warning for container shipping
items.summary: Dr Raymon Krishnan, president of Singapore’s Logistics & Supply Chain Management Society, writes for Splash today, reflecting on one of this week’s most talked about stories in the mainstream press. On Wednesday, the 990-foot ocean liner SS United States was deliberately sunk off Destin, Florida, to become what is expected to be the world’s largest artificial reef. Initial underwater inspections found the vessel upright, approximately 180 feet below the surface. Its retirement offers a useful perspective on container shipping as it now faces another turning point. The container shipping industry is preparing for a significant increase in fleet capacity. According to Drewry’s third-quarter 2026 Container Forecaster the global containership orderbook stood at approximately 13.9m teu on 1 September 2026, equivalent to 40.9% of the active fleet. Aviation permanently changed the market for passenger liners, while container shipping remains essential to trade. Conversion into an artificial reef offers a potential tourism and conservation role but it is neither a universal nor necessarily economical solution for commercial vessels. It is to ensure there is a commercially sustainable reason to put them to work.

items.original_title: UK blacklists 11 ships in fresh Russia sanctions sweep
items.summary: Britain has slapped fresh sanctions on 11 ships linked to Russian energy exports, targeting five LNG carriers, five oil tankers and a floating storage unit in its latest effort to disrupt Moscow’s seaborne oil and gas trade. The measures also cover nine companies, including Russian oil producer Slavneft, Rosneft’s Vostok Oil project and several energy trading businesses based in Dubai. The latest vessel additions include LNG carriers Melicertes, Neleus, Perle, Aeolus and Oneiroi , alongside the Novatek-linked Koryak FSU . The restrictions prohibit the specified ships from accessing British ports and impose controls on chartering and operating them. Dubai-based Forteza Trading, Patera and Novus Energy have been designated, with British authorities specifically linking Novus Energy to dealings involving vessels already subject to UK restrictions. Russian petrochemical producer Sibur and coal groups SUEK and Kuzbassrazrezugol also feature in the latest package. The move brings all ten of Russia’s largest oil producers under British sanctions following the inclusion of Slavneft. The government announced the measures during the European Political Community summit in Dublin, where pressure on Russian energy revenues formed part of discussions on Ukraine. Britain has been steadily expanding its maritime restrictions this year, including sanctions against six ships in August and an earlier package targeting Russia’s developing LNG shadow fleet.

items.title: Baltic Exchange and Mercuria await verdict in landmark tanker index trial
items.original_title: Baltic Exchange and Mercuria await verdict in landmark tanker index trial
items.summary: One of shipping’s most consequential legal battles has concluded in London, with the Baltic Exchange and commodities trader Mercuria awaiting a High Court ruling on whether the industry’s leading VLCC freight benchmark should have continued operating after war erupted in the Middle East. At the centre of the dispute is TD3C, the Baltic’s benchmark for transporting crude from Ras Tanura in Saudi Arabia to Ningbo, China, a voyage requiring passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Mercuria has argued that the disruption following the outbreak of hostilities on February 28 rendered the benchmark unreliable, with insufficient physical tanker activity to support meaningful assessments. The trading house maintains that the Baltic failed to meet its statutory and contractual obligations by continuing to publish rates despite mounting evidence that its contributing shipbrokers could not reliably determine a market price. During the trial, Mercuria highlighted internal communications revealing considerable uncertainty among Baltic staff and broker panellists. In closing arguments, the Baltic accused Mercuria of repeatedly changing its case and suggested the litigation was an attempt to escape the consequences of unsuccessful trading positions. The Baltic has also warned that retrospective intervention in a widely used benchmark could create significant uncertainty for freight derivatives and physical shipping contracts linked to TD3C. The Baltic Exchange has consistently defended its benchmark procedures and regulatory compliance.

items.original_title: Singapore-flagged cargo ship strikes US bridge
items.summary: A Singapore-flagged cargoship has struck a bridge spanning the Delaware River between Philadelphia and New Jersey, forcing its closure and renewing concerns about the vulnerability of American bridges to vessel collisions. The 180 m Strategic Alliance, a handysize bulk carrier built in 2013, hit the Tacony-Palmyra Bridge at approximately 1.15pm local time on Thursday while its draw span was open for marine traffic. The impact damaged part of the bridge and initially prevented the structure from closing, causing extensive traffic delays on both sides of the river. The vessel subsequently moored at a Kinder Morgan terminal in Bristol, Pennsylvania, where US Coast Guard inspectors attended. The bridge, which opened in 1929 and carries up to 76,200 vehicles daily, reopened around 8.40pm, with one lane remaining closed for repairs. The incident comes as American authorities seek to strengthen protection for bridges following the March 2024 Dali disaster in Baltimore, when a containership, also Singapore-flagged, struck the Francis Scott Key Bridge, causing its collapse and killing six construction workers. In September, the US Coast Guard published a major review examining bridge and port infrastructure vulnerabilities across 11 ports, producing 20 recommendations for improving maritime risk management. Maryland is also pursuing a $177m programme to strengthen the Chesapeake Bay Bridge against ship strikes, including new protective structures around its supporting piers.

items.title: Dry bulk ship recycling falls 36% to 18-year low
items.original_title: Dry bulk ship recycling falls 36% to 18-year low
items.summary: Dry bulk ship recycling has been at a low level since 2021 due to strong freight rates. These include high congestion in 2021, longer sailing distances due to sanctions on Russian coal, which caused ships to be rerouted away from the Red Sea, and growing shipments from the Atlantic to Asia. “Following several years of low ship recycling levels, a significant overhang has built up. As ships remain in service for longer, the dry bulk fleet has gradually aged, with the average bulk carrier now over 13 years old, compared with an average of 10 years at the start of the decade,” says Gouveia. There are now 1,035 dry bulk ships, totalling 46.7m DWT, which are more than 25 years old. In our latest Dry Bulk Shipping Market Overview & Outlook, we forecast the supply/demand balance to gradually weaken in 2027 and 2028, albeit from a high baseline. Ship deliveries are expected to accelerate, growing 19% in 2027 and a further 4% in 2028. Consequently, we estimate ship recycling could increase to 5.5m DWT in 2027 and 9.2m DWT in 2028, which would be the highest since 2020. Nevertheless, even with this increase, recycling levels would be low compared with the highs seen during the 2010s and an overhang of older ships would remain,” says Gouveia.

items.title: Why shipowners might be better off sharing profits than taking on debt
items.original_title: Why shipowners might be better off sharing profits than taking on debt
items.summary: Traditional loans demand repayments regardless of freight markets. Earnings-sharing structures offer a different proposition: investors participate in a vessel’s fortunes while owners retain control. Captain Vikas Pandey from Shipfinex explains. Small and mid-sized owners, who by one industry estimate own up to 60% of the world’s ships, still meet low advance ratios on older tonnage, higher margins, or alternative lenders asking for equity kickers and profit participation on top of interest. Earnings-sharing tends to make sense where bank debt is unavailable or priced close to equity; where the vessel has visible employment, such as a period charter, that investors can underwrite; where the owner needs to protect liquidity through the cycle; or where equity is locked in an unencumbered vessel that the owner wants to release without selling. Before signing, owners should settle the definition of net earnings and deductible costs, the treatment of off-hire and drydocking, reserve funding, the term and any cap on investor returns, buy-back rights, and what happens on a sale or total loss. Where a first-priority registered ship mortgage is in place, the mortgagee’s consent is required and investor distributions rank behind debt service. Debt remains the cheapest capital in shipping for owners who can get it on good terms.

items.title: NYK charts the great reshuffling of global commodity trades
items.original_title: NYK charts the great reshuffling of global commodity trades
items.summary: One of the world’s largest shipowners has given its take on where it sees the gas, dry bulk, and tanker markets heading in the coming years. The global VLCC fleet will see a significant expansion despite the extraordinary earnings currently being enjoyed by tanker owners, with Japanese shipping giant Nippon Yusen Kaisha (NYK) forecasting the delivery of approximately 290 supertankers between 2026 and 2029. NYK’s research group unveiled its latest shipping market outlook yesterday, predicting that the active VLCC fleet will increase from 909 vessels at the end of 2025 to 1,082 by the end of 2029, a rise of 19%. The forecast assumes a substantial number of ageing vessels will leave the market, but deliveries are expected to be comparable to those witnessed during the shipping boom of the 2000s. NYK’s research also anticipates a fundamental restructuring of global commodity trades over the coming decade. Seaborne iron ore volumes are forecast to decline from 1.65bn tonnes in 2025 to 1.40bn tonnes in 2035 as Chinese steel production contracts. Coal shipments are forecast to fall from 1.33bn tonnes to 1.04bn tonnes over the same period, with thermal coal accounting for most of the decline. LNG is heading in the opposite direction, with seaborne volumes expected to climb from 433m tonnes to 622m tonnes by 2035.

Splash reported on November 3 that Singapore VLSFO had climbed back above $1,000 a tonne for the first time since March, with the Iran conflict having almost doubled bunker prices since February. Despite the latest retreat, Singapore fuel remains approximately 56% more expensive than immediately before the war began on February 28. items.title: Singapore Strait robbery spike sparks fresh security warning
items.original_title: Singapore Strait robbery spike sparks fresh security warning
items.summary: A sudden resurgence in robberies aboard merchant ships in the Singapore Strait has prompted regional maritime security authorities to issue an urgent warning, with three vessels boarded in nine days and one seafarer injured. The ReCAAP Information Sharing Centre issued an incident alert yesterday following attacks on two bulk carriers and a tanker between November 2 and 10, warning that further incidents are possible. All three robberies occurred in the eastbound lane of the Traffic Separation Scheme, within approximately 3.2 nautical miles of each other. The first incident involved the bulk carrier Star Calypso, boarded at 2125 hrs on November 2. The second, involving the bulk carrier APJ Priti 2, took place late on November 4, followed by an attack on the tanker Salsa in the early hours of November 10. The latest incidents bring the number of robberies reported in the Straits of Malacca and Singapore this year to 28. ReCAAP is urging Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore to intensify patrols and surveillance, improve coordination and share intelligence to identify and arrest those responsible. Shipmasters have been advised to maintain heightened vigilance, particularly during darkness, and strengthen preventive measures, including CCTV coverage of potential boarding locations. The organisation is also encouraging vessels to report suspicious activity immediately and use its digital reporting and incident mapping systems when assessing voyage risks.

A changing China, resilient emerging economies and a relatively predictable fleet supply picture will be among the biggest themes shaping dry bulk shipping when the industry gathers in Geneva next April, according to Ivar Hansson Myklebust. On technology, Myklebust sees opportunities less in revolutionary developments than in improving everyday shipping processes, from maintenance planning to freight collection. items.summary: The UK is moving ahead with a £90 million investment in autonomous underwater systems, advanced sensors and artificial intelligence to strengthen the Royal Navy’s ability to track Russian submarines and protect critical infrastructure in the North Atlantic. The initiative, known as Atlantic Net, is the first operational phase of the Royal Navy’s broader Atlantic Bastion programme, which aims to combine crewed warships and submarines with autonomous systems to improve underwater surveillance and counter potential threats to subsea communications cables, energy networks and shipping routes. The UK Ministry of Defence announced the investment Tuesday during the International Sea Power Conference in Oslo, Norway, alongside a framework agreement with UK-based marine robotics company Ocean Infinity Solutions. The system will combine underwater sensors, uncrewed platforms, communications technology and AI-powered data analysis to detect and track potentially hostile submarine activity. The programme is expected to become operational in 2027, according to UK Defence Minister Luke Pollard, who outlined the plans in a speech in Oslo. “This investment gives the Royal Navy new technology to find threats earlier and protect our critical infrastructure, while also backing British business.” The investment comes amid growing concern among European governments and NATO allies over the vulnerability of underwater infrastructure, particularly communications cables and energy connections that are essential to both civilian economies and military operations.

That remains an art rather than science, but indicates how the container shipping industry has experienced something of a paradigm shift into an era in which waves of mega-congestion ripple across the port and shipping system. Terminal occupancy levels – ie, how many containers are sitting in a yard awaiting either a truck or loading on a vessel – continue to sit way above what these facilities were designed to handle. Some of this is beyond terminal operators’ control – they have no say over when vessels arrive, or how delayed they might have been at the previous port; while wars, weather, and other disruptive events are in the hands of the gods – or people who think of themselves as such… However, in the spirit of supply chain resilience, they could be far better prepared to tackle congestion when it arises.

items.title: Hapag’s standalone Asia-Mexico string adds another spoke to Gemini hub network
items.original_title: Hapag’s standalone Asia-Mexico string adds another spoke to Gemini hub network
items.summary: Hapag-Lloyd has presented AMX, its new Asia–Mexico service, as standalone: its own ships; its own rotation of Ningbo-Qingdao-Busan-Ensenada-Manzanillo-Lázaro Cárdenas-Ningbo; launching in January 2027. Standalone is the word the press release leans on, and it is the one worth questioning. AMX is standalone the way a spoke is standalone – Hapag owns the vessels, but it can only fill an 8,000 teu ship on this run because the Gemini hub network it operates with Maersk gives the cargo somewhere to come from. The hub-and-spoke network it now runs with Maersk supplies the missing pieces – balancing cargo through the Gemini hubs and relay connections onward, so AMX does not have to source a full, self-sufficient ship at Asian load ports. The simple answer to ‘why standalone’ and ‘why 2027’ is that the network to support a self-controlled spoke only recently came together. Each is an owned loop made to clip onto the Gemini backbone, and the method is consistent — control the vessel, fill it through the hubs. That slice is not small: I estimate Hapag’s allocation on MSC’s loops is worth around 8,375 teu of nominal vessel capacity, call it some 7,000 teu of usable space for its customers once a ship is realistically loaded.

items.title: Panama Canal turns the taps back on

items.summary: The Panama Canal has raised its daily transit capacity to 34 vessels and increased the maximum allowable draft for neopanamax ships to 50 ft, marking another significant easing of restrictions following an exceptionally wet October. The Panama Canal Authority (ACP) confirmed that an additional booking slot for super-category vessels at the original panamax locks would increase their daily allocation from 18 to 19. Total availability now stands at 24 slots through the panamax locks and 10 through the larger neopanamax locks, up from a combined 33 previously. The maximum neopanamax draft has meanwhile increased from 49 ft to 50 ft (15.24 m), effective immediately and until further notice. Data compiled by Ursa Shipbrokers showed Gatun Lake averaged 85.80 ft (26.15 m) during October, just 0.15 ft below its historical average and more than 6 ft higher than during the drought-stricken October of 2023. Rainfall across the canal watershed during the first 29 days of October was 8.4% above the 30-year average and 83.6% greater than the corresponding period three years ago. The turnaround is particularly striking given the dire outlook during August, when weak rainfall and a strengthening El Niño forced authorities to slash daily booking capacity to 32 vessels and impose tighter draft restrictions.

items.title: ‘Severe supply imbalance’ threat as record box ship deliveries loom
items.original_title: ‘Severe supply imbalance’ threat as record box ship deliveries loom
items.summary: The global containership fleet is set to expand by almost 50% by 2030, with even record levels of vessel scrapping unlikely to prevent a severe supply imbalance. In its latest report, Sea-Intelligence forecast the fleet will grow from almost 34m teu today to 40m teu by Q2 28, and 50m teu by the Q3 30. The analyst expects average annual fleet growth of 10% between 2027 and 2030, based on existing orders, with further newbuilding contracts potentially increasing that figure. Quarterly deliveries are forecast to average 1m teu over the period, peaking at 1.8m teu in the third quarter of 2028. This compares with average quarterly deliveries of 560,000 teu between 2023 and 2026, highlighting the scale of capacity due to enter the market. In 2016, carriers scrapped a record 670,000 teu, equivalent to just 3.3% of the fleet, during the industry’s previous overcapacity crisis. Jonathan Roach, analyst at Braemar, told The Loadstar there were 1,944 vessels aged 20 years or more, with 1,903 ships on order. Jan Tiedemann, VP liner strategy at Alphaliner, told The Loadstar he expected scrapping to increase in 2027 and 2028 without offsetting the newbuilding influx. He also pointed to the replacement needs of larger vessels built between 2000 and 2010, many of which will approach the end of their commercial lives in the mid-2030s.

items.title: UK offshore supply chain looks overseas for growth
items.original_title: UK offshore supply chain looks overseas for growth
items.summary: The UK’s offshore energy supply chain is increasingly looking overseas for new business as uncertainty surrounding domestic projects threatens investment, jobs and specialist engineering capacity, according to a new industry report. Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) found that just 35% of 60 companies surveyed were confident about their UK business prospects over the next 12 months. Meanwhile, 80% expect more future investment and growth to come from international markets. The findings form part of OEUK’s Supply Chain Report 2026, which examines the pressures facing engineering companies, manufacturers, vessel operators, logistics providers, and other businesses supporting offshore energy developments. The trade body identified approximately £123bn ($165.5bn) of potential UK offshore energy capital investment between 2026 and 2035 but warned that many projects remain uncertain. According to the report, 95% of companies surveyed believe they could expand capacity if domestic offshore activity increased. OEUK warned that offshore wind, carbon capture, and other emerging energy markets have not yet generated sufficient activity to replace traditional oil and gas work at scale. Katy Heidenreich, OEUK’s supply chain and people director, called for continued investment in domestic oil and gas alongside renewable energy developments. OEUK cautioned that losing specialist offshore capabilities now could leave the UK increasingly dependent on overseas suppliers when future energy projects move into construction.

The dispute concerned a demurrage claim, valued at approximately US$48,000, which the owners were pursuing against charterers for delays at discharge. The shipbroker became involved after failing to pass on supporting documents relating to the claim. However, the broker’s delay in forwarding key documents meant the charterers’ objections did not reach the owners promptly, reducing the opportunity to address any deficiencies in the claim. Given the weaknesses in the underlying demurrage claim, the matter was settled with the shipbroker contributing US$24,000, half the value of the claim, towards the owners’ losses. “In this case, the delay reduced the owners’ chance to deal with problems in their claim early. Expert support in assessing liability and negotiating a resolution can make a real difference to the result. Demurrage claims often carry tight contractual time bars, so claims and supporting documents should be passed on as soon as they arrive, with a record of when that happened. Even a short delay can prejudice a party’s position and prove costly.” Source: International Transport Intermediaries Club (ITIC)

The network was first proposed at the G7 leaders’ summit in Évian, France, in June, when leaders issued a joint declaration identifying maritime transport as the primary route for international drug and precursor chemical trafficking. According to France’s Foreign Ministry , the network is holding its first meeting in Marseille alongside the November 9–10 G7 ministerial gathering in Paris. items.summary: HMM has declared general average following the fire aboard the HMM Platinum , generating a slew of new hurdles for cargo owners, with the carrier still seeking a port of refuge for the vessel, which has spent the past month anchored off the South African coast. Korhi Average Adjusters & Surveyors have been appointed to handle the adjustment for the 5,593 teu containership, with Korhi and Richards Hogg Lindley responsible for collecting general average security. Those with cargo aboard will be required to provide salvage security and general average security before shipments can be forwarded or released, while uninsured cargo owners will be required to provide cash deposits, although the amounts have yet to be determined. Given the extent of cargo damage and timetable for discharging containers remains unclear, the requirements add more uncertainty for forwarders and their customers with shipments aboard the vessel. Fire broke out aboard the Liberian-flagged vessel on 6 October, while sailing from Kattupalli to Santos, with reports claiming that the blaze originated in a container while the ship was off Madagascar’s southern coast, with some 2,300 boxes aboard. Salvage specialist SMIT was appointed under a Lloyd’s Open Form agreement, while the vessel diverted towards South Africa but finding a suitable port of refuge has proved complicated.

items.title: India’s coking coal import dependence on Australia falls to 54%
items.original_title: India’s coking coal import dependence on Australia falls to 54%
items.summary: India’s dependence on Australia for coking coal imports fell to 54% in 2025 from 73% in 2019, according to a deposition by the steel ministry to a parliamentary standing committee. About 90% of India’s coking coal requirement, a key raw material for steelmaking via the BF-BOF route, is met through imports because India has limited availability of high-quality, low-ash coking coal. Australia remains India’s largest source of coking coal imports, but the share of Russia rose from 0.62% to 8.15%, the US from 8% to 17%, Mozambique from 4% to 7.31% and Indonesia from 2.46% to 4%. India’s steel sector imported 58 Mt of coking coal in FY25, up from 57 Mt in FY24, at a cost of around Rs 1.5 lakh crore. Under the Aatmanirbhar Coal Mission, the government’s Mission Coking Coal targets 140 Mt of domestic raw coking coal production by 2030 – 105 Mt from Coal India Limited and 35 Mt from private allocations – while aiming to raise the blending ratio of domestic coal in steelmaking from 10% to 30%. Globally, high-quality hard coking coal is concentrated in a few countries, and Australia accounts for more than 50% of internationally traded coking coal owing to its high-quality reserves, stable mining ecosystem and efficient logistics. Combined with an estimated 8% effective capacity boost from the return of Asia-Europe services to the Suez Canal, cumulative supply growth could exceed 50% by the end of the decade. The consultancy calculates that quarterly newbuilding deliveries will average 1m teu between 2027 and 2030, peaking at an extraordinary 1.8m teu in the third quarter of 2028. By 2030, some 10.8m teu will be aboard ships older than 20 years, although Sea-Intelligence doubts carriers intend to scrap anything approaching that figure. The warnings follow a similarly bearish forecast from Xeneta, which expects fleet growth of 6.8% next year against demand growth of just 2.5% to 4%.

items.original_title: LA Port Strike Threat Deferred Again As Labor Talks Drag On
items.summary: Shipping containers sit on a Maersk vessel docked at the port of Los Angeles in Long Beach, California, U.S., March 10, 2026. REUTERS/Caroline Brehman Nov 7, 2026 (Bloomberg) –The union representing about 250 security workers at the US’s busiest ports agreed to continue negotiations on a new labor contract for two more weeks, their employers said. The latest extension goes through Nov. 20, with additional talks scheduled with the International Longshore and Warehouse Union Local 26 scheduled during that period, the Pacific Maritime Association said in a statement. Disruptions at the affected terminals could impact roughly 85% of the cargo that moves through the Port of Long Beach and a third of the cargo at the Port of Los Angeles, according to the PMA. The previous labor contract expired in July 2025, though the PMA, which represents port terminals and ocean carriers, and ILWU Local 26 have been meeting regularly to negotiate with the assistance of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service. 27 that ILWU dockworkers and marine clerks — who have separate labor contracts and are not party to this dispute — were expected to stand with the Local 26 watchmen in the event of a strike.

items.title: Soaring Freight Rates Give US Refiners Edge As Crude Discounts Widen
items.original_title: Soaring Freight Rates Give US Refiners Edge As Crude Discounts Widen
items.summary: The Houston Ship Channel and adjacent refineries, part of the Port of Houston, are seen in Houston, Texas, U.S., May 5, 2019. REUTERS/Loren Elliott Nov 6 (Reuters) – The Iran conflict has sent tanker rates soaring, forcing sellers to deepen discounts on heavy crude grades and giving US Gulf Coast refiners a cost advantage over Asian rivals, executives said after reporting bumper third-quarter profits. The disruption particularly benefited US Gulf Coast refiners, which could buy discounted heavy crude produced closer to home, including from Canada and Venezuela, while Asian rivals faced sharply higher freight and insurance costs to import similar grades through longer and riskiershipping routes. Rising freight costs have widened discounts on Canadian heavy crude, including Western Canadian Select (WCS), which typically trades below US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI), creating a windfall for Gulf Coast refiners, as more than 70% of their facilities are configured to process heavier crude. Freight costs for shipping crude from the US Gulf Coast to Asia have jumped to $30-$35 a barrel from about $5 a year earlier, Hawkins said. “Higher freight rates actually give us an advantage into the typical export markets into Latin America,” said Gary Simmons, chief operating officer of Valero, adding that it mainly competes with European barrels in that market.
